newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council may vote this week on top U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council may vote this week on top U.N. post.

text.p: With Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali having stepped aside in the race for the top U.N. post, the Security Council is expected to begin voting this week on African candidates vying for his job.
Four candidates were officially nominated on Friday and at least one more contender is expected to enter the race before the council convenes on Monday afternoon.

Its president, Paulo Fulci of Italy, said the 15-seat body hoped to decide on Monday when to begin a series of informal votes before official balloting starts. He said the council would discuss the issue again on Wednesday.
Any winning candidate has to get at least nine votes and no veto from one of the five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France.

But in the Byzantine U.N. procedures, members can vote for more than one candidate and a veto does not necessarily preclude another vote -- and another veto -- on the same candidate. Any candidate approved by the council must be endorsed by the 185-member General Assembly.

On November 19, Washington cast the sole negative vote against Boutros-Ghali for a second five-year term, saying he was slow to initiate reforms for the world body and that he was unpopular in the Republican-dominated U.S. Congress.
The secretary-general last Wednesday opened the door for other African candidates by suspending his candidacy "temporarily." He is not expected to enter the race unless there is a deadlock.

But the council, including the United States, said preference would be given to an African in line with a tradition that each continent serves two terms. Boutros-Ghali, a 74-year old Egyptian, ends his five-year term on December 31.

The four nominated on Friday were: Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of Islamic Conference; Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast; and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, the former U.N. special envoy for Burundi who is executive secretary of the Washington-based Global Coalition for Africa.
Salim A. Salim of Tanzania, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity, is expected to enter the race on Monday, South African President Nelson Mandela said.
Mandela, speaking in Cape Town on Sunday also brought into stark relief what some delegates are calling the language war.

He said French President Jacques Chirac told him by telephone that he would veto Salim because he was not fluent in French as well as English and Chirac was not prepared to support any candidate without these qualifications.
Mandela also said he tried in vain to convince U.S. President Bill Clinton to drop his opposition to Boutros-Ghali, who was endorsed by the OAU at its July summit in Yaounde, Cameroon.
Since Washington vetoed Boutros-Ghali, a Paris-educated former deputy foreign minister backed by France, French envoys have insisted a "francophone" fill the post.

Other candidates who may enter the race this week are Senagal's foreign minister, Moutapha Niassi, Olara Otunnu, a former Ugandan U.N. ambassador who heads the New York-based International Peace Academy; and Wally N'Dow of Gambia, assistant secretary-general in charge of the U.N. Centre for Human Settlements in Nairobi.

The United States has not declared for any candidate, realising that the anger generated by its veto of Boutros-Ghali would jeopardise the chances of any nominee it supported. But both Washington and London are expected to insist on a high-degree of fluency in Engish.
